summary:
Tennessee law regulates gender presentation in public. The Adult Entertainment Act of 2023 (SB 3/HB 9) defines "adult cabaret entertainment" to include male or female impersonators and makes it a criminal offence on public property or anywhere a child could see it. A first offence is a Class A misdemeanour carrying up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine; a second violation is a Class E felony with one to six years and fines to $3,000. A federal judge declared the statute vague and overbroad and unconstitutional in June 2023, but it was reinstated on procedural grounds after appeal, and in 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to it, leaving the appeals-court ruling upholding the law in force. A separate suit remains ongoing.

Facilities access is restricted by birth sex. The "Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act," passed in April 2026, requires transgender people to use only facilities matching sex assigned at birth, bars trans women from women's shelters, and mandates that transgender inmates be housed by sex assigned at birth. Earlier provisions remain part of the statutory background: legislation of 2 May 2019 defines a transgender person using a bathroom corresponding with gender identity as committing indecent exposure, and May 2021 laws banned transgender students from public-school bathrooms matching their identity and required small businesses permitting transgender use of multi-person bathrooms to post warning signs under penalty of up to six months' jail. The business-sign requirement took effect 1 July 2021, was enjoined on 9 July 2021 and struck down entirely in May 2022 as a First Amendment violation; the school bathroom law drew further lawsuits from August 2021.

Gender-affirming medical care for minors is prohibited. Senate Bill 1, signed 1 March 2023, makes it illegal to provide such care to any person under 18 in Tennessee or through out-of-state telehealth. New care was barred after 1 July 2023 and existing care had to be withdrawn by 31 March 2024. The statute authorises regret-based lawsuits by parents, guardians and physicians, and $25,000 suits by the Attorney General against providers. The U.S. Department of Justice challenged the law with the ACLU and Lambda Legal on 26 April 2023; a partial injunction of 28 June 2023 was stayed on 8 July 2023, and the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the statute 6-3 in United States v. Skrmetti on 18 June 2025, holding it did not violate equal protection. A May 2024 law adds civil penalties for adults who help minors obtain such care elsewhere, and April 2024 legislation bans the care for inmates.

Custody is a site of specific harm. In April 2024 the Tennessee State Legislature passed a bill banning gender-affirming care for people held in state prisons, and under the 2026 Act transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons according to sex assigned at birth.

Identity documents are governed by a fixed statutory definition of sex. Tennessee has prohibited change of sex on an original birth certificate under Tenn. Code Ann. § 68-3-203(d) since 1977, and a 2023 law signed by Governor Lee defines "sex" as determined by anatomy and genetics existing at the time of birth. The Department of Safety denied a legally transitioned transgender woman a driver's licence gender change, prompting an ACLU suit filed 23 April 2024 in Davidson County.

Transgender students are excluded from school sport. Legislation of 26 March 2021 banning transgender youth athletes passed the Senate 27-6 and the House 71-16 with 5 abstentions; Public Chapter 1005 of 22 April 2022 requires proof of gender assigned at birth under threat of funding loss. Litigation over a Farragut student barred from boys' golf produced partial summary judgment on 29 March 2024. Public Chapter 448 of May 2023 shields teachers from suit and discipline for using birth-certificate pronouns, and a May 2024 mandatory-outing law took effect immediately requiring teachers to report to administrators, and administrators to parents, whenever a child requests a different name or pronoun.

Protection machinery is thin and partly federal. Tennessee's hate-crime statute has punished bias based on sexual orientation since 2001 without explicitly listing gender identity; a February 2019 Attorney General opinion holds that selecting a victim because she is transgender qualifies for enhancement under § 40-35-114(17) as an offence committed because of gender, and federal law covers gender-identity bias. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity is prohibited through Title VII as applied in R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes v. EEOC (Sixth Circuit, 7 March 2018) and Bostock v. Clayton County (14 June 2020), but state law provides no statutory ban on sexual orientation or gender identity discrimination, and local public-employment ordinances in Knoxville, Memphis, Franklin, Chattanooga and Nashville/Davidson County do not reach private employers and are blocked by the Equal Access to Intrastate Commerce Act.

Violence risk carries a documented mitigation in law. The gay and trans panic defence remains available to lower or eliminate punishment for fatal attacks, and reporting describes police and legal officials sympathetic to aggressors who turn a blind eye, calling same-sex attraction a sin. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation recorded 0 anti-transgender incidents in 2019, 1 in 2020 and 2 in 2021; these are raw counts with no population denominator and no evidence of continued reporting after 2021. In April 2021 Tennessee was described as experiencing economic and social impacts similar to the 2016 North Carolina bathroom-law backlash, and in 2024 the Human Rights Campaign classified Tennessee among the lowest-ranking states for LGBTQ rights.

Marriage and shelter access carry direct exclusions. Marriage licences have been issued to same-sex couples since Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, but HB 878, signed 21 February 2024, allows government employees to refuse to solemnize a marriage against their personal beliefs. Trans women are barred from women's shelters under the 2026 Act.
